w1.title: Worked Example 1: Structured Rows, Columns & Validation Rules
w1.question: Audit a 5-row Jal Seva water log where Row 3 has a negative litre reading (−40 L).

steps.text: Check range constraint: water saved must be ≥ 0 L.
Flag Row 3 (−40 L) as a sign-entry error against the paper receipt (40 L).
Correct Row 3 to +40 L and recompute the column sum.

check.q: Which check prevents a typist from entering text inside a 'Litres Saved' numeric column?

opts.m: Visual styling does not block invalid data entry.
Use field validation rules to enforce numeric input.

w2.title: Worked Example 2: Checksum Totals & Cross-Foot Balancing
w2.question: Three cohorts saved 120 L, 150 L, and 130 L of water. Verify the batch total.

steps.text: Add Cohort A + Cohort B: 120 + 150 = 270 L.
Confirm that the summary row matches 400 L before syncing.

check.q: What does a mismatch between the row-sum and column-sum in a spreadsheet indicate?

opts.t: A formula range or data-entry error in at least one cell

opts.m: Row and column sums must always be mathematically identical.

opts.t: The file size is too small
opts.m: Cross-foot mismatches always signal a calculation or range omission.

w3.title: Worked Example 3: Tamper-Evident Offline Sync & Receipt Hashing
w3.question: Why do we store a SHA-256 hash alongside each offline cohort export pack?

steps.text: Compute the hash of the JSON payload before saving to local storage.
Recompute the hash on the Centre Server upon upload.
If both hashes match, the ledger batch is verified intact.

check.q: If even one digit in a ledger file changes, what happens to its SHA-256 hash?

opts.t: The hash changes completely, alerting the verifier

opts.m: Cryptographic hashes exhibit the avalanche effect.
Any byte change produces a completely different SHA-256 digest.
